summary: This pedagogical review integrates pulse-shaping physics, analytical derivations via the Magnus expansion, and practical hardware considerations for superconducting-qubit control. The paper reconstructs quantum gate implementation from first principles, covering single-qubit DRAG pulses, hardware signal generation (AWG, LO, IQ mixing), and multi-qubit cross-resonance gates with error-suppression sequences.
motivation: Students transitioning from abstract quantum gates to experimental superconducting-qubit implementation lack a unified narrative connecting theoretical Hamiltonian engineering to hardware realities and the systematic error channels that emerge at each order of perturbation theory.
method: The authors use the Magnus expansion to identify error channels order-by-order in a three-level transmon model, derive the DRAG quadrature condition $Q = -\dot{I}(t)/\Delta$ to cancel first-order leakage, analyze hardware imperfections (finite sampling, LO phase noise, IQ skew), and trace pulse-engineering strategies for the cross-resonance gate including echo sequences, active cancellation, and multi-derivative DRAG.
result: The framework shows how finite pulse bandwidth produces $\sigma_{12}^{\pm}$ leakage at first order and residual $\sigma_{01}^y$ rotation errors that DRAG suppresses; AC Stark $\sigma_{01}^z$ phase errors appear at second order; for CR gates, echo sequences eliminate $Z \otimes Z$, $Z \otimes I$, and $I \otimes X$ terms, while multi-derivative DRAG achieving $\approx 0.997$ fidelity combines recursive corrections on levels $|0\rangle$–$|1\rangle$, $|1\rangle$–$|2\rangle$, and the $|0\rangle$–$|2\rangle$ two-photon transition.
